# Rate Limits

Rate limits act as control measures to regulate how frequently users and applications can access our API within specified timeframes. These limits help ensure service stability, fair access, and protection
against misuse so that we can serve reliable and fast inference for all.

## Understanding Rate Limits

Rate limits are measured in:

* **RPM:** Requests per minute
* **RPD:** Requests per day
* **TPM:** Tokens per minute
* **TPD:** Tokens per day
* **ASH:** Audio seconds per hour
* **ASD:** Audio seconds per day
* **ITPM:** Input tokens per minute
* **OTPM:** Output tokens per minute

Cached tokens do not count towards your rate limits.

Rate limits apply at the organization level, not individual users. You can hit any limit type depending on which threshold you reach first.

**Example:** Let's say your RPM = 50 and your TPM = 200K. If you were to send 50 requests with only 100 tokens within a minute, you would reach your limit even though you did not send 200K tokens within those
50 requests.

### Input and Output Token Rate Limits (ITPM / OTPM)

In addition to the combined TPM limit, some organizations are also subject to separate per-minute limits on input tokens (ITPM) and output tokens (OTPM). For example, an OTPM limit caps how many completion tokens your organization can generate per minute, regardless of how many input tokens are sent.

If these limits are configured on your account, you'll see your TPM value on the Limits page — hover over it to see the **"X in / Y out"** breakdown. If no breakdown appears, your organization has a single combined TPM cap with no separate input/output limits.

## Rate Limits

The following is a high level summary and there may be exceptions to these limits. You can view the current, exact rate limits for your organization on the limits page in your account settings.

**Need higher rate limits?** Upgrade to Developer plan to access higher limits, Batch and Flex processing, and more. Note that the limits shown below are the base limits for the Developer plan, and higher limits are available for select workloads and enterprise use cases.

|  | | | | | |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MODEL ID | RPM | RPD | TPM | TPD | ASH | ASD |

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| canopylabs/orpheus-arabic-saudi | 10 | 100 | 1.2K | 3.6K | - | - |
| canopylabs/orpheus-v1-english | 10 | 100 | 1.2K | 3.6K | - | - |
| meta-llama/llama-prompt-guard-2-22m | 30 | 14.4K | 15K | 500K | - | - |
| meta-llama/llama-prompt-guard-2-86m | 30 | 14.4K | 15K | 500K | - | - |
| openai/gpt-oss-120b | 30 | 1K | 8K | 200K | - | - |
| openai/gpt-oss-20b | 30 | 1K | 8K | 200K | - | - |
| openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b | 3 | 1K | 2K | 200K | - | - |
| qwen/qwen3.8-27b | 30 | 1K | 8K | 200K | - | - |
| whisper-large-v3 | 20 | 2K | - | - | 7.2K | 28.8K |
| whisper-large-v3-turbo | 20 | 2K | - | - | 7.2K | 28.8K |

## Rate Limit Headers

In addition to viewing your limits on your account's limits page, you can also view rate limit information such as remaining requests and tokens in HTTP response
headers as follows:

The following headers are set (values are illustrative):

| Header | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| retry-after | 2 | In seconds |
| x-ratelimit-limit-requests | 14400 | Always refers to Requests Per Day (RPD) |
| x-ratelimit-limit-tokens | 18000 | Always refers to Tokens Per Minute (TPM) |
| x-ratelimit-remaining-requests | 14370 | Always refers to Requests Per Day (RPD) |
| x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens | 17997 | Always refers to Tokens Per Minute (TPM) |
| x-ratelimit-reset-requests | 2m59.56s | Always refers to Requests Per Day (RPD) |
| x-ratelimit-reset-tokens | 7.66s | Always refers to Tokens Per Minute (TPM) |

## Handling Rate Limits

When you exceed rate limits, our API returns a `429 Too Many Requests` HTTP status code.

**Note**: `retry-after` is only set if you hit the rate limit and status code 429 is returned. The other headers are always included.

These limits help maintain fair usage, protect against abuse, and help maintain system performance for all users. {% button href="https://aistudio.google.com/rate-limit?timeRange=last-28-days" variant="primary" %}View your active rate limits in AI Studio{% /button %} ## How rate limits work {% id="how-rate-limits-work" %} Rate limits are usually measured across three dimensions: \* Requests per minute (\*\*RPM\*\*) \* Tokens per minute (input) (\*\*TPM\*\*) \* Requests per day (\*\*RPD\*\*) Your usage is evaluated against each limit, and exceeding any of them will trigger a rate limit error. For example, if your RPM limit is 20, making 21 requests within a minute will result in an error, even if you haven't exceeded your TPM or other limits. Rate limits are applied per project, not per API key. Requests per day (\*\*RPD\*\*) quotas reset at midnight Pacific time. Limits vary depending on the specific model being used, and some limits only apply to specific models. For example, Images per minute, or IPM, is only calculated for models capable of generating images (Nano Banana), but is conceptually similar to TPM. Other models might have a token per day limit (TPD). Built-in tools also have specific rate limits. For example, Grounding with Google Search on Gemini 3 and newer models is subject to a default limit of 1,500 requests per day (RPD) per project on the Gemini Developer API (see [Grounding with Google Search](/docs/google-search#pricing)). Rate limits are more restricted for experimental and preview models. ### Spend-based rate limits {% id="spend-rate-limits" %} In addition to requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) limits, the Gemini API enforces spend-based rate limits to protect against unexpected charges. Whether these limits apply to your account depends on your billing history and [usage tier](/docs/rate-limits#usage-tiers). The following table shows the spend-based rate limits for each [usage tier](/docs/rate-limits#usage-tiers). These limits are evaluated on a rolling 10-minute window. Whether these limits apply to your account depends on your billing history and account standing. | Usage tier | Spend rate limit (per 10 minutes) | | :--- | :--- | | \*\*Free\*\* | N/A | | \*\*Tier 1\*\* | $10 | | \*\*Tier 2\*\* | $200 | | \*\*Tier 3\*\* | $200 | If you hit a spend-based rate limit, the API returns a `429 RESOURCE\_EXHAUSTED` error. To resolve this: \* Wait and retry after a short period. \* Reduce the rate of expensive requests, for example by using smaller context windows or shorter outputs. \* If you consistently hit this limit during normal usage, [request a rate limit increase](/docs/rate-limits#request-rate-limit-increase). ## Usage tiers {% id="usage-tiers" %} Rate limits are tied to the project's usage tier. As your API usage and spending increase, you'll be automatically upgraded to a higher tier with increased rate limits. The qualifications for Tiers 2 and 3 are based on the total cumulative spending on Google Cloud services (including, but not limited to, the Gemini API) for the billing account linked to your project. | Usage tier | Qualification | [Billing tier cap](/docs/billing#tier-spend-caps) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | \*\*Free\*\* | [Active project](/docs/api-key#google-cloud-projects) or free trial | N/A | | \*\*Tier 1\*\* | [Set up and link an active billing account](/docs/billing#setup-billing) | $250 | | \*\*Tier 2\*\* | Paid $100 + 3 days from first successful payment | $2,000 | | \*\*Tier 3\*\* | Paid $1,000 + 30 days from first successful payment | $20,000 - $100,000+ | While meeting the stated qualification criteria is generally sufficient for approval, in rare cases an upgrade request may be denied based on other factors identified during the review process. This system helps maintain the security and integrity of the Gemini API platform for all users. ## Gemini API rate limits {% id="current-rate-limits" %} Rate limits depend on a variety of factors (such as your usage tier) and can be viewed in Google AI Studio. For life sciences research, explore the Rosalind Academic Plan.

# Pricing

See pricing for our business and enterprise plans.

### Business

A secure workspace with company context and flexible seat types for any budget.

Get started(opens in a new window)

#### Standard seat

$20/ month

Best for everyday work

$20/month if billed annually. $25/month if billed monthly.

#### Premium seat

$100/ month

More usage than standard, with no 5-hour limit

$100/month if billed annually. $125/month if billed monthly.

What’s included:

* All ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex features
* Access across desktop, web, and mobile
* Connect to Google Workspace, Slack, GitHub, Microsoft 365, and more
* Secure workspace with SAML, SSO, and MFA
* Centralized billing and administration
* Usage analytics and spend controls
* No training on your business data by default
* Workspace agents for customized workflows
* Mix and match seat types

For teams of 2–200 employees. Unlimited subject to abuse guardrails. Learn more⁠⁠(opens in a new window).

Starting in December, plan usage will have a shared limit across all of ChatGPT and Codex. Learn more⁠(opens in a new window).

### Enterprise

Enterprise-grade AI, security, and support for businesses operating at scale

Contact sales

#### Custom pricing

Contact our sales team to discuss enterprise pricing.\*

What’s included:

* Expanded context window that supports longer inputs and larger files
* Enterprise-level security and controls, including SCIM, EKM, user analytics, domain verification, and role-based access controls
* Advanced data privacy with custom data retention policies, encryption at rest and in transit, and no training on your business data by default. Learn more⁠
* Support for data residency in ten regions
* 24/7 priority support, SLAs, custom legal terms, and access to AI advisors (eligible customers)
* Invoicing and billing, volume discounts

\*Credit-based⁠⁠(opens in a new window) pricing and token-based⁠(opens in a new window) pricing are available for Enterprise plans.

### Looking for personal plans?

Visit ChatGPT.com for consumer pricing

Learn more(opens in a new window)

blocks.text: Yes. Spend caps are on by default on the Pro Plan. You can turn spend caps off for usage beyond the Plan limits to pay as you grow.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: Spend caps are on by default and you need to toggle them off from your dashboard to enable pay as you grow pricing.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: Our Pro Plan is charged up front, and billed on a monthly basis. Additional usage costs are also billed at the end of the month.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: Supabase applies sales tax, VAT, GST, and other indirect taxes where required by law, based on your billing address. For more details, see our Billing FAQ.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: Pricing may change in the future. As a team of developers, we are committed to keeping our pricing as developer friendly as possible.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: The organization is allocated credits for unused time during the billing month. Those credits can be used for other projects.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: You can track your organization's usage at any time on the usage page in the dashboard, which shows how each project is tracking against your plan's limits. Your upcoming invoice on the billing page updates as you go, and organizations on the Pro Plan or above can use the Spend cap to control costs.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: You can create two projects, one for development and one for production — the Free Plan includes two free projects. You can also use Branching, available on the Pro Plan and above, to run a separate development environment off your production project.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: Yes, you can use the Docker setup or the Supabase CLI. Supabase Studio is also available in the Docker setup.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: Yes, you can pause a project at any time. Our Free Plan gives you 2 free projects, but you can have as many paused projects as you want. Just pause and unpause them as needed.

blocks.heading_path: Predictable pricing, designed to scale > Frequently asked questions
blocks.text: Yes. If your organization has an AWS spend commitment (such as a PPA or EDP), you can buy Pro or Team through AWS Marketplace so eligible Supabase spend counts toward that commitment. Billing details and plan management then run through AWS, and Spend Cap is unavailable for AWS-managed organizations. Learn more on our AWS Marketplace page, or go straight to the public listing.

blocks.text: Can't find the answer to your question? Open a support ticket to receive help from our team.

Yes. Spend caps are on by default on the Pro Plan. You can turn spend caps off for usage beyond the Plan limits to pay as you grow.

Spend caps are on by default and you need to toggle them off from your dashboard to enable pay as you grow pricing.

Our Pro Plan is charged up front, and billed on a monthly basis. Additional usage costs are also billed at the end of the month.

Supabase applies sales tax, VAT, GST, and other indirect taxes where required by law, based on your billing address. For more details, see our Billing FAQ.

Pricing may change in the future. As a team of developers, we are committed to keeping our pricing as developer friendly as possible.

The organization is allocated credits for unused time during the billing month. Those credits can be used for other projects.

You can track your organization's usage at any time on the usage page in the dashboard, which shows how each project is tracking against your plan's limits. Your upcoming invoice on the billing page updates as you go, and organizations on the Pro Plan or above can use the Spend cap to control costs.

You can create two projects, one for development and one for production — the Free Plan includes two free projects. You can also use Branching, available on the Pro Plan and above, to run a separate development environment off your production project.

Yes, you can use the Docker setup or the Supabase CLI. Supabase Studio is also available in the Docker setup.

Yes, you can pause a project at any time. Our Free Plan gives you 2 free projects, but you can have as many paused projects as you want. Just pause and unpause them as needed.

Yes. If your organization has an AWS spend commitment (such as a PPA or EDP), you can buy Pro or Team through AWS Marketplace so eligible Supabase spend counts toward that commitment. Billing details and plan management then run through AWS, and Spend Cap is unavailable for AWS-managed organizations. Learn more on our AWS Marketplace page, or go straight to the public listing.

blocks.text: Render charges for three things: your workspace plan (flat subscription), metered features like bandwidth (usage-based), and compute for your applications (usage-based).

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: Compute plans are set at a per-service basis, and billing is prorated to the second. If you create a web service on a paid compute plan and turn it off 24 hours later, you are only billed for 24 hours of compute. This also applies to service types that spin up and shut down automatically, like Cron Jobs and Workflows. You are only billed for compute when these services are actively running your workload.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: If a workspace has no services (live or suspended) and no activity during a month, the workspace subscription fee for that month will be waived.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: Scale and Enterprise plans let you create multiple workspaces within the same organization to better manage multiple teams. Our team is happy to help you determine the best way to organize your teams on Render. Contact us here.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: Your workspace's builds and other pre-deploy tasks use Render compute resources. Pipeline minutes track the duration of these tasks. You can view your pipeline usage from your dashboard's Billing page.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: With a Professional plan or higher, you can enable the Performance pipeline to run builds on larger compute instances, with an additional corresponding charge for pipeline minutes.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: With Render’s Free compute plans, you can spin up web services, Render Key Value instances, and Render Postgres databases at no charge. Free compute plans types have usage limits and are designed to help you to explore new tech, build personal projects, and preview Render's developer experience.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: We accept all major credit and debit cards. Your payment info is stored and processed securely by Stripe and never touches our servers.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: A $1 USD transaction is performed as a credit security check to ensure your card details are correct and authorized. The charge is refunded after the transaction completes.

blocks.heading_path: root
blocks.text: Render does not offer full migration professional services. However, you can find a certified solution partner through our expert network.

blocks.text: Great! We're always around to help. You can email us any time at support@render.com, or talk to us in our user community.

## Questions & Answers

### 

We recommend Premium for new AI users, Super for daily agent users, and Ultra for power users. Plus is recommended for social creators with limited AI usage. The Teams plan is recommended for professionals collaborating with others, and larger organizations that need invoicing, pooled usage, or advanced security should choose Enterprise.

### 

Self-serve plans support all major credit and debit cards. For invoice-based billing and wire transfers, please contact us to discuss the Enterprise plan.

### 

Every tier includes a pool of AI usage shared across Cursor and Grok. Within Grok, the pool covers Chat, Imagine, Voice, and Bot. Higher tiers include larger pools, and usage costs vary by product. Your allowance refreshes weekly, so one heavy day never wipes out your whole month.

If you reach your included usage, you can keep going with top-offs, or wait for your allowance to refresh. You'll always see your remaining usage in settings. See our docs for more details.

### 

Paid plans include Grok API access. API usage is billed separately at standard model rates and doesn't draw from your plan's usage pool. See model pricing.

### 

Plus includes Grok models only. Premium and above include generous usage of Grok models but do not include an allowance for third-party models. Third-party models remain available in Cursor at API list price. You pay for exactly what you use, and you can set spending caps to manage costs.

### 

All prices are exclusive of any applicable taxes. See our Subscription Terms for more information.

### 

Admins can access usage information and key metrics through the Admin Dashboard.

### 

Privacy mode can be enabled in settings or by a team admin. When it is enabled, we guarantee that code data is not used for training by us or our model providers. You can learn more on our Security page.

### 

No. Subscriptions are only sold directly through X Subscription Corp. We do not authorize any resellers or third-party sellers. blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What is GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot is an AI coding agent that helps you write, understand, and ship software. It helps you across every step of the software development lifecycle including exploring your codebase, planning your project, automating your workflows, reviewing your changes, and resolving merge conflicts.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What is GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: Because Copilot is built into GitHub, it works within the development workflow you already use:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What is GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: * Your code and its history.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What is GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: * The issues and pull requests you already use to track work.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What is GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: * The automations you run in your repository.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What is GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: A change can start as an issue, be picked up by an agent, return as a pull request, get reviewed for quality and security, and be merged. You and Copilot work on it in the same place, with the same context, instead of moving code into separate tools and back again.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What languages, IDEs, and surfaces does GitHub Copilot support?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot is trained on all languages that appear in public repositories.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What languages, IDEs, and surfaces does GitHub Copilot support?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot is available in multiple IDEs including Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, XCode, Vim, Neovim, Zed, and Eclipse. GitHub Copilot is also available in the terminal/CLI, through the GitHub Copilot desktop app, on the web, on mobile, in Slack, and in Teams. You can easily start working on one surface and continue the same session on another. Learn more here.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How can I get started using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: You can find a plethora of resources on GitHub Docs including quickstart guides for multiple surfaces and best practices. Our community has built Awesome GitHub Copilot to share reusable agents, skills, instructions, hooks, and tools built by developers to help you ship faster with Copilot. You can also find tutorials and YouTube videos to help you get started today!

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are GitHub AI Credits?
blocks.text: GitHub AI Credits are how you pay for AI usage in GitHub Copilot. Every plan includes a monthly allowance: 1 AI credit = $0.01 USD.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are GitHub AI Credits?
blocks.text: You use credits when you chat with Copilot and work with agents. Code completions and next edit suggestions don't use credits. They remain unlimited with every paid plan.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are GitHub AI Credits?
blocks.text: How many credits an interaction uses depends on the model you choose and the complexity of the task. A quick question to a lightweight model costs a fraction of a credit. A longer agent session on a frontier model across many files costs more.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are the differences between the Free, Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot has multiple offerings for organizations and individual developers. Key differences between the plans include total GitHub AI Credits and available models. To see more information and a comparison chart between plans, please see our plans & pricing page.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: When you've used your monthly allowance, you have a few options:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: * Wait for your next cycle. Your included allowance resets every month.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: * Keep working with paid usage. Set a dollar budget for additional usage and Copilot continues without interruption. Credits draw down at $0.01 each, so a $10 budget covers 1,000 credits.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: * Switch to a less expensive model. Lightweight models use fewer credits per interaction and stretch your remaining allowance further.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: On GitHub Copilot Business and GitHub Copilot Enterprise, admins set usage limits and decide whether additional paid usage is allowed. If it isn't, Copilot pauses until the next cycle.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: You can track your usage and reset date in your Copilot settings, with alerts at 75%, 90%, and 100% of any configured budget.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What is included in GitHub Copilot Free?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot Free users are limited to 2,000 completions and access to entry level models per month. If you're on the Free plan, you can upgrade to Pro through your Copilot settings page or directly on the Copilot marketing page.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot processes personal data based on how Copilot is accessed and used: whether via GitHub.com, mobile app, extensions, or one of various IDE extensions, or through features like suggestions for the command line interface (CLI), IDE code completions, or personalized chat on GitHub.com. The types of personal data processed may include:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **User Engagement Data:** This includes pseudonymous identifiers captured on user interactions with Copilot, such as accepted or dismissed completions, error messages, system logs, and product usage metrics.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **Prompts:** These are inputs for chat or code, along with context, sent to Copilot's AI to generate suggestions.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **Suggestions:** These are the AI-generated code lines or chat responses provided to users based on their prompts.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **Feedback Data:** This comprises real-time user feedback, including reactions (e.g., thumbs up/down) and optional comments, along with feedback from support tickets.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: How GitHub uses Copilot data depends on how the user accesses Copilot and for what purpose. GitHub generally uses personal data to:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Deliver, maintain, and update the services as per the customer's configuration and usage, to ensure personalized experiences and recommendations

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Troubleshoot, which involves preventing, detecting, resolving, and mitigating issues, including security incidents and product-related problems, by fixing software bugs and maintaining the online services' functionality and up-to-dateness

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Enhance user productivity, reliability, effectiveness, quality, privacy, accessibility, and security by keeping the service current and operational

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: These practices are outlined in GitHub’s Data Protection Agreement (DPA), which details our data handling commitments to our data controller customers. GitHub also uses certain personal data with customer authorization under the DPA, for the following purposes:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Billing and account management

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * To comply with and resolve legal obligations

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * For abuse detection, prevention, and protection, virus scanning, and scanning to detect violations of terms of service

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * To generate summary reports for calculating employee commissions and partner incentives

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * To produce aggregated reports for internal use and strategic planning, covering areas like forecasting, revenue analysis, capacity planning, and product strategy.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: To learn more, read more at our Copilot Trust Center.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: GitHub uses the Copilot data from Individual subscribers for all the operational purposes described above for Business/Enterprise subscribers.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: **In addition, for Individual subscribers only:** GitHub may use Copilot interaction data — including prompts (inputs), **s**uggestions (outputs), and code snippets generated during Copilot sessions — to train and improve AI models. This training helps improve code suggestions for all Copilot users.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: Individual subscribers can opt out of having their data used for AI model training at any time through https://github.com/settings/copilot/features. Opting out does not affect your access to Copilot features.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: For details on GitHub's data processing activities as a controller, particularly for Copilot Free, Copilot Pro, and Copilot Pro customers, refer to the GitHub Terms of Service and the GitHub Privacy Statement.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot support compliance with the GDPR and other data protection laws?
blocks.text: Yes. GitHub and customers can enter a Data Protection Agreement that supports compliance with the GDPR and similar legislation.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot ever output personal data?
blocks.text: While we've designed GitHub Copilot with privacy in mind, the expansive definition of personal data under legislation like the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) means we can't guarantee it will never output such data. The Large Language Model (LLM) powering GitHub Copilot was trained on public code and there were instances in our tests where the tool made suggestions resembling personal data. These suggestions were typically synthesized and not tied to real individuals.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > How does Copilot allow users to access, alter or delete personal data?
blocks.text: These actions are available to Copilot users as described in the GitHub Privacy Statement.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: The primary IP considerations for GitHub Copilot relate to copyright. The model that powers Copilot is trained on a broad collection of publicly accessible code, which may include copyrighted code, and Copilot’s suggestions (in rare instances) may resemble the code its model was trained on. Here’s some basic information you should know about these considerations:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: Copyright law permits the use of copyrighted works to train AI models:  Countries around the world have provisions in their copyright laws that enable machines to learn, understand, extract patterns, and facts from copyrighted materials, including software code. For example, the European Union, Japan, and Singapore, have express provisions permitting machine learning to develop AI models. Other countries including Canada, India, and the United States also permit such training under their fair use/fair dealing provisions. GitHub Copilot’s AI model was trained with the use of code from GitHub’s public repositories—which are publicly accessible and within the scope of permissible copyright use.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: What about copyright risk in suggestions? In rare instances (less than 1% based on GitHub’s research), suggestions from GitHub may match examples of code used to train GitHub’s AI model. Again, Copilot does not “look up” or “copy and paste” code, but is instead using context from a user’s workspace to synthesize and generate a suggestion.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: Our experience shows that matching suggestions are most likely to occur in two situations: (i) when there is little or no context in the code editor for Copilot’s model to synthesize, or (ii) when a matching suggestion represents a common approach or method. If a code suggestion matches existing code, there is risk that using that suggestion could trigger claims of copyright infringement, which would depend on the amount and nature of code used, and the context of how the code is used. In many ways, this is the same risk that arises when using any code that a developer does not originate, such as copying code from an online source, or reusing code from a library. That is why responsible organizations and developers recommend that users employ code scanning policies to identify and evaluate potential matching code.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: In Copilot, you can opt whether to allow Copilot to suggest code completions that match publicly available code on GitHub.com. For more information, see "Configuring GitHub Copilot settings on GitHub.com". If you have allowed suggestions that match public code, GitHub Copilot can provide you with details about the matching code when you accept such suggestions. Matching code does not necessarily mean copyright infringement, so it is ultimately up to the user to determine whether to use the suggestion, and what and who to attribute (along with other license compliance) in appropriate circumstances.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: Yes, GitHub Copilot does include an optional code referencing filter to detect and suppress certain suggestions that match public code on GitHub.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: GitHub has created a duplication detection filter to detect and suppress suggestions that contain code segments over a certain length that match public code on GitHub. This filter can be enabled by the administrator for your enterprise and it can apply for all organizations within your enterprise, or the administrator can defer control to individual organizations.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: With the filter enabled, Copilot checks code suggestions for matches or near-matches against public code on GitHub of 65 lexemes or more (on average,150 characters). If there is a match, the suggestion will not be shown to the user.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot also includes filters to block offensive language in the prompts and to avoid synthesizing suggestions in sensitive contexts. We continue to work on improving the filter system to more intelligently detect and remove offensive outputs. If you see offensive outputs, please report them directly to copilot-safety@github.com so that we can improve our safeguards. GitHub takes this challenge very seriously and we are committed to addressing it.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: In addition to off-topic, harmful, and offensive output filters, GitHub Copilot also scans the outputs for vulnerable code.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Can GitHub Copilot introduce insecure code in its suggestions?
blocks.text: Public code may contain insecure coding patterns, bugs, or references to outdated APIs or idioms. When GitHub Copilot synthesizes code suggestions based on this data, it can also synthesize code that contains these undesirable patterns. Copilot has filters in place that either block or notify users of insecure code patterns that are detected in Copilot suggestions. These filters target the most common vulnerable coding patterns, including hardcoded credentials, SQL injections, and path injections. Additionally, in recent years we’ve provided tools such as GitHub Advanced Security, GitHub Actions, Dependabot, and CodeQL to open source projects to help improve code quality. Of course, you should always use GitHub Copilot together with good testing and code review practices and security tools, as well as your own judgment.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Is GitHub Copilot intended to fully automate code generation and replace developers?
blocks.text: No. GitHub Copilot is a tool intended to make developers more efficient. It’s not intended to replace developers.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Is GitHub Copilot intended to fully automate code generation and replace developers?
blocks.text: Developers should use exactly the same sorts of safeguards and diligence with Copilot’s suggestions as they would use with any third-party code.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Is GitHub Copilot intended to fully automate code generation and replace developers?
blocks.text: Practices such as rigorous functionality testing, code scanning, security testing, etc. should continue policies with Copilot’s suggestions. Moreover, you should make sure your code editor or editor does not automatically compile or run generated code before you review it.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Does GitHub Copilot support accessibility features?
blocks.text: We are conducting internal testing of GitHub Copilot’s ease of use by developers with disabilities and working to ensure that GitHub Copilot is accessible to all developers. Learn more about accessibility at GitHub and view our detailed documentation on various accessibility topics and features, including instructions for using our products with screen readers and other assistive technologies at our GitHub Accessibility website.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Frequently asked questions > Will GitHub Copilot work as well using languages other than English?
blocks.text: Given public sources are predominantly in English, GitHub Copilot will likely work less well in scenarios where natural language prompts provided by the developer are not in English and/or are grammatically incorrect. Therefore, non-English speakers might experience a lower quality of service.

blocks.text: You use credits when you chat with Copilot and work with agents. Code completions and next edit suggestions don't use credits. They remain unlimited with every paid plan.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What are GitHub AI Credits?
blocks.text: How many credits an interaction uses depends on the model you choose and the complexity of the task. A quick question to a lightweight model costs a fraction of a credit. A longer agent session on a frontier model across many files costs more.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What are the differences between the Free, Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot has multiple offerings for organizations and individual developers. Key differences between the plans include total GitHub AI Credits and available models. To see more information and a comparison chart between plans, please see our plans & pricing page.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: When you've used your monthly allowance, you have a few options:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: * Wait for your next cycle. Your included allowance resets every month.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: * Keep working with paid usage. Set a dollar budget for additional usage and Copilot continues without interruption. Credits draw down at $0.01 each, so a $10 budget covers 1,000 credits.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: * Switch to a less expensive model. Lightweight models use fewer credits per interaction and stretch your remaining allowance further.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: On GitHub Copilot Business and GitHub Copilot Enterprise, admins set usage limits and decide whether additional paid usage is allowed. If it isn't, Copilot pauses until the next cycle.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What happens when I hit my usage limit?
blocks.text: You can track your usage and reset date in your Copilot settings, with alerts at 75%, 90%, and 100% of any configured budget.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Plans & pricing > What is included in GitHub Copilot Free?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot Free users are limited to 2,000 completions and access to entry level models per month. If you're on the Free plan, you can upgrade to Pro through your Copilot settings page or directly on the Copilot marketing page.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot processes personal data based on how Copilot is accessed and used: whether via GitHub.com, mobile app, extensions, or one of various IDE extensions, or through features like suggestions for the command line interface (CLI), IDE code completions, or personalized chat on GitHub.com. The types of personal data processed may include:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **User Engagement Data:** This includes pseudonymous identifiers captured on user interactions with Copilot, such as accepted or dismissed completions, error messages, system logs, and product usage metrics.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **Prompts:** These are inputs for chat or code, along with context, sent to Copilot's AI to generate suggestions.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **Suggestions:** These are the AI-generated code lines or chat responses provided to users based on their prompts.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?
blocks.text: * **Feedback Data:** This comprises real-time user feedback, including reactions (e.g., thumbs up/down) and optional comments, along with feedback from support tickets.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: How GitHub uses Copilot data depends on how the user accesses Copilot and for what purpose. GitHub generally uses personal data to:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Deliver, maintain, and update the services as per the customer's configuration and usage, to ensure personalized experiences and recommendations

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Troubleshoot, which involves preventing, detecting, resolving, and mitigating issues, including security incidents and product-related problems, by fixing software bugs and maintaining the online services' functionality and up-to-dateness

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Enhance user productivity, reliability, effectiveness, quality, privacy, accessibility, and security by keeping the service current and operational

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: These practices are outlined in GitHub’s Data Protection Agreement (DPA), which details our data handling commitments to our data controller customers. GitHub also uses certain personal data with customer authorization under the DPA, for the following purposes:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * Billing and account management

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * To comply with and resolve legal obligations

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * For abuse detection, prevention, and protection, virus scanning, and scanning to detect violations of terms of service

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * To generate summary reports for calculating employee commissions and partner incentives

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: * To produce aggregated reports for internal use and strategic planning, covering areas like forecasting, revenue analysis, capacity planning, and product strategy.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?
blocks.text: To learn more, read more at our Copilot Trust Center.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: GitHub uses the Copilot data from Individual subscribers for all the operational purposes described above for Business/Enterprise subscribers.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: **In addition, for Individual subscribers only:** GitHub may use Copilot interaction data — including prompts (inputs), **s**uggestions (outputs), and code snippets generated during Copilot sessions — to train and improve AI models. This training helps improve code suggestions for all Copilot users.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: Individual subscribers can opt out of having their data used for AI model training at any time through https://github.com/settings/copilot/features. Opting out does not affect your access to Copilot features.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?
blocks.text: For details on GitHub's data processing activities as a controller, particularly for Copilot Free, Copilot Pro, and Copilot Pro customers, refer to the GitHub Terms of Service and the GitHub Privacy Statement.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > Does GitHub Copilot support compliance with the GDPR and other data protection laws?
blocks.text: Yes. GitHub and customers can enter a Data Protection Agreement that supports compliance with the GDPR and similar legislation.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > Does GitHub Copilot ever output personal data?
blocks.text: While we've designed GitHub Copilot with privacy in mind, the expansive definition of personal data under legislation like the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) means we can't guarantee it will never output such data. The Large Language Model (LLM) powering GitHub Copilot was trained on public code and there were instances in our tests where the tool made suggestions resembling personal data. These suggestions were typically synthesized and not tied to real individuals.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Privacy > How does Copilot allow users to access, alter or delete personal data?
blocks.text: These actions are available to Copilot users as described in the GitHub Privacy Statement.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: The primary IP considerations for GitHub Copilot relate to copyright. The model that powers Copilot is trained on a broad collection of publicly accessible code, which may include copyrighted code, and Copilot’s suggestions (in rare instances) may resemble the code its model was trained on. Here’s some basic information you should know about these considerations:

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: Copyright law permits the use of copyrighted works to train AI models:  Countries around the world have provisions in their copyright laws that enable machines to learn, understand, extract patterns, and facts from copyrighted materials, including software code. For example, the European Union, Japan, and Singapore, have express provisions permitting machine learning to develop AI models. Other countries including Canada, India, and the United States also permit such training under their fair use/fair dealing provisions. GitHub Copilot’s AI model was trained with the use of code from GitHub’s public repositories—which are publicly accessible and within the scope of permissible copyright use.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: What about copyright risk in suggestions? In rare instances (less than 1% based on GitHub’s research), suggestions from GitHub may match examples of code used to train GitHub’s AI model. Again, Copilot does not “look up” or “copy and paste” code, but is instead using context from a user’s workspace to synthesize and generate a suggestion.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: Our experience shows that matching suggestions are most likely to occur in two situations: (i) when there is little or no context in the code editor for Copilot’s model to synthesize, or (ii) when a matching suggestion represents a common approach or method. If a code suggestion matches existing code, there is risk that using that suggestion could trigger claims of copyright infringement, which would depend on the amount and nature of code used, and the context of how the code is used. In many ways, this is the same risk that arises when using any code that a developer does not originate, such as copying code from an online source, or reusing code from a library. That is why responsible organizations and developers recommend that users employ code scanning policies to identify and evaluate potential matching code.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?
blocks.text: In Copilot, you can opt whether to allow Copilot to suggest code completions that match publicly available code on GitHub.com. For more information, see "Configuring GitHub Copilot settings on GitHub.com". If you have allowed suggestions that match public code, GitHub Copilot can provide you with details about the matching code when you accept such suggestions. Matching code does not necessarily mean copyright infringement, so it is ultimately up to the user to determine whether to use the suggestion, and what and who to attribute (along with other license compliance) in appropriate circumstances.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: Yes, GitHub Copilot does include an optional code referencing filter to detect and suppress certain suggestions that match public code on GitHub.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: GitHub has created a duplication detection filter to detect and suppress suggestions that contain code segments over a certain length that match public code on GitHub. This filter can be enabled by the administrator for your enterprise and it can apply for all organizations within your enterprise, or the administrator can defer control to individual organizations.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: With the filter enabled, Copilot checks code suggestions for matches or near-matches against public code on GitHub of 65 lexemes or more (on average,150 characters). If there is a match, the suggestion will not be shown to the user.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: GitHub Copilot also includes filters to block offensive language in the prompts and to avoid synthesizing suggestions in sensitive contexts. We continue to work on improving the filter system to more intelligently detect and remove offensive outputs. If you see offensive outputs, please report them directly to copilot-safety@github.com so that we can improve our safeguards. GitHub takes this challenge very seriously and we are committed to addressing it.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?
blocks.text: In addition to off-topic, harmful, and offensive output filters, GitHub Copilot also scans the outputs for vulnerable code.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Can GitHub Copilot introduce insecure code in its suggestions?
blocks.text: Public code may contain insecure coding patterns, bugs, or references to outdated APIs or idioms. When GitHub Copilot synthesizes code suggestions based on this data, it can also synthesize code that contains these undesirable patterns. Copilot has filters in place that either block or notify users of insecure code patterns that are detected in Copilot suggestions. These filters target the most common vulnerable coding patterns, including hardcoded credentials, SQL injections, and path injections. Additionally, in recent years we’ve provided tools such as GitHub Advanced Security, GitHub Actions, Dependabot, and CodeQL to open source projects to help improve code quality. Of course, you should always use GitHub Copilot together with good testing and code review practices and security tools, as well as your own judgment.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Is GitHub Copilot intended to fully automate code generation and replace developers?
blocks.text: No. GitHub Copilot is a tool intended to make developers more efficient. It’s not intended to replace developers.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Is GitHub Copilot intended to fully automate code generation and replace developers?
blocks.text: Developers should use exactly the same sorts of safeguards and diligence with Copilot’s suggestions as they would use with any third-party code.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Is GitHub Copilot intended to fully automate code generation and replace developers?
blocks.text: Practices such as rigorous functionality testing, code scanning, security testing, etc. should continue policies with Copilot’s suggestions. Moreover, you should make sure your code editor or editor does not automatically compile or run generated code before you review it.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Does GitHub Copilot support accessibility features?
blocks.text: We are conducting internal testing of GitHub Copilot’s ease of use by developers with disabilities and working to ensure that GitHub Copilot is accessible to all developers. Learn more about accessibility at GitHub and view our detailed documentation on various accessibility topics and features, including instructions for using our products with screen readers and other assistive technologies at our GitHub Accessibility website.

blocks.heading_path: Take flight with GitHub Copilot > Pricing plans > Responsible AI > Will GitHub Copilot work as well using languages other than English?
blocks.text: Given public sources are predominantly in English, GitHub Copilot will likely work less well in scenarios where natural language prompts provided by the developer are not in English and/or are grammatically incorrect. Therefore, non-English speakers might experience a lower quality of service.

### Frequently asked questions

#### General

#### What is GitHub Copilot?

GitHub Copilot is an AI coding agent that helps you write, understand, and ship software. It helps you across every step of the software development lifecycle including exploring your codebase, planning your project, automating your workflows, reviewing your changes, and resolving merge conflicts.

Because Copilot is built into GitHub, it works within the development workflow you already use:

* Your code and its history.
* The issues and pull requests you already use to track work.
* The automations you run in your repository.

A change can start as an issue, be picked up by an agent, return as a pull request, get reviewed for quality and security, and be merged. You and Copilot work on it in the same place, with the same context, instead of moving code into separate tools and back again.

#### What languages, IDEs, and surfaces does GitHub Copilot support?

GitHub Copilot is trained on all languages that appear in public repositories.

GitHub Copilot is available in multiple IDEs including Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, XCode, Vim, Neovim, Zed, and Eclipse. GitHub Copilot is also available in the terminal/CLI, through the GitHub Copilot desktop app, on the web, on mobile, in Slack, and in Teams. You can easily start working on one surface and continue the same session on another. Learn more here.

#### How can I get started using GitHub Copilot?

You can find a plethora of resources on GitHub Docs including quickstart guides for multiple surfaces and best practices. Our community has built Awesome GitHub Copilot to share reusable agents, skills, instructions, hooks, and tools built by developers to help you ship faster with Copilot. You can also find tutorials and YouTube videos to help you get started today!

#### Plans & pricing

#### What are GitHub AI Credits?

GitHub AI Credits are how you pay for AI usage in GitHub Copilot. Every plan includes a monthly allowance: 1 AI credit = $0.01 USD.

You use credits when you chat with Copilot and work with agents. Code completions and next edit suggestions don't use credits. They remain unlimited with every paid plan.

How many credits an interaction uses depends on the model you choose and the complexity of the task. A quick question to a lightweight model costs a fraction of a credit. A longer agent session on a frontier model across many files costs more.

#### What are the differences between the Free, Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans?

GitHub Copilot has multiple offerings for organizations and individual developers. Key differences between the plans include total GitHub AI Credits and available models. To see more information and a comparison chart between plans, please see our plans & pricing page.

#### What happens when I hit my usage limit?

When you've used your monthly allowance, you have a few options:

* Wait for your next cycle. Your included allowance resets every month.
* Keep working with paid usage. Set a dollar budget for additional usage and Copilot continues without interruption. Credits draw down at $0.01 each, so a $10 budget covers 1,000 credits.
* Switch to a less expensive model. Lightweight models use fewer credits per interaction and stretch your remaining allowance further.

On GitHub Copilot Business and GitHub Copilot Enterprise, admins set usage limits and decide whether additional paid usage is allowed. If it isn't, Copilot pauses until the next cycle.

You can track your usage and reset date in your Copilot settings, with alerts at 75%, 90%, and 100% of any configured budget.

#### What is included in GitHub Copilot Free?

GitHub Copilot Free users are limited to 2,000 completions and access to entry level models per month. If you're on the Free plan, you can upgrade to Pro through your Copilot settings page or directly on the Copilot marketing page.

#### Privacy

#### What personal data does GitHub Copilot process?

GitHub Copilot processes personal data based on how Copilot is accessed and used: whether via GitHub.com, mobile app, extensions, or one of various IDE extensions, or through features like suggestions for the command line interface (CLI), IDE code completions, or personalized chat on GitHub.com. The types of personal data processed may include:

* **User Engagement Data:** This includes pseudonymous identifiers captured on user interactions with Copilot, such as accepted or dismissed completions, error messages, system logs, and product usage metrics.
* **Prompts:** These are inputs for chat or code, along with context, sent to Copilot's AI to generate suggestions.
* **Suggestions:** These are the AI-generated code lines or chat responses provided to users based on their prompts.
* **Feedback Data:** This comprises real-time user feedback, including reactions (e.g., thumbs up/down) and optional comments, along with feedback from support tickets.

#### How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Business and Enterprise Subscribers?

How GitHub uses Copilot data depends on how the user accesses Copilot and for what purpose. GitHub generally uses personal data to:

* Deliver, maintain, and update the services as per the customer's configuration and usage, to ensure personalized experiences and recommendations
* Troubleshoot, which involves preventing, detecting, resolving, and mitigating issues, including security incidents and product-related problems, by fixing software bugs and maintaining the online services' functionality and up-to-dateness
* Enhance user productivity, reliability, effectiveness, quality, privacy, accessibility, and security by keeping the service current and operational

These practices are outlined in GitHub’s Data Protection Agreement (DPA), which details our data handling commitments to our data controller customers. GitHub also uses certain personal data with customer authorization under the DPA, for the following purposes:

* Billing and account management
* To comply with and resolve legal obligations
* For abuse detection, prevention, and protection, virus scanning, and scanning to detect violations of terms of service
* To generate summary reports for calculating employee commissions and partner incentives
* To produce aggregated reports for internal use and strategic planning, covering areas like forecasting, revenue analysis, capacity planning, and product strategy.

To learn more, read more at our Copilot Trust Center.

#### How does GitHub use the Copilot data from Individual (Free/Pro/Pro+) Subscribers?

GitHub uses the Copilot data from Individual subscribers for all the operational purposes described above for Business/Enterprise subscribers.

**In addition, for Individual subscribers only:** GitHub may use Copilot interaction data — including prompts (inputs), **s**uggestions (outputs), and code snippets generated during Copilot sessions — to train and improve AI models. This training helps improve code suggestions for all Copilot users.

Individual subscribers can opt out of having their data used for AI model training at any time through https://github.com/settings/copilot/features. Opting out does not affect your access to Copilot features.

For details on GitHub's data processing activities as a controller, particularly for Copilot Free, Copilot Pro, and Copilot Pro customers, refer to the GitHub Terms of Service and the GitHub Privacy Statement.

#### Does GitHub Copilot support compliance with the GDPR and other data protection laws?

Yes. GitHub and customers can enter a Data Protection Agreement that supports compliance with the GDPR and similar legislation.

#### Does GitHub Copilot ever output personal data?

While we've designed GitHub Copilot with privacy in mind, the expansive definition of personal data under legislation like the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) means we can't guarantee it will never output such data. The Large Language Model (LLM) powering GitHub Copilot was trained on public code and there were instances in our tests where the tool made suggestions resembling personal data. These suggestions were typically synthesized and not tied to real individuals.

#### How does Copilot allow users to access, alter or delete personal data?

These actions are available to Copilot users as described in the GitHub Privacy Statement.

#### Responsible AI

#### What are the intellectual property considerations when using GitHub Copilot?

The primary IP considerations for GitHub Copilot relate to copyright. The model that powers Copilot is trained on a broad collection of publicly accessible code, which may include copyrighted code, and Copilot’s suggestions (in rare instances) may resemble the code its model was trained on. Here’s some basic information you should know about these considerations:

Copyright law permits the use of copyrighted works to train AI models:  Countries around the world have provisions in their copyright laws that enable machines to learn, understand, extract patterns, and facts from copyrighted materials, including software code. For example, the European Union, Japan, and Singapore, have express provisions permitting machine learning to develop AI models. Other countries including Canada, India, and the United States also permit such training under their fair use/fair dealing provisions. GitHub Copilot’s AI model was trained with the use of code from GitHub’s public repositories—which are publicly accessible and within the scope of permissible copyright use.

What about copyright risk in suggestions? In rare instances (less than 1% based on GitHub’s research), suggestions from GitHub may match examples of code used to train GitHub’s AI model. Again, Copilot does not “look up” or “copy and paste” code, but is instead using context from a user’s workspace to synthesize and generate a suggestion.

Our experience shows that matching suggestions are most likely to occur in two situations: (i) when there is little or no context in the code editor for Copilot’s model to synthesize, or (ii) when a matching suggestion represents a common approach or method. If a code suggestion matches existing code, there is risk that using that suggestion could trigger claims of copyright infringement, which would depend on the amount and nature of code used, and the context of how the code is used. In many ways, this is the same risk that arises when using any code that a developer does not originate, such as copying code from an online source, or reusing code from a library. That is why responsible organizations and developers recommend that users employ code scanning policies to identify and evaluate potential matching code.

In Copilot, you can opt whether to allow Copilot to suggest code completions that match publicly available code on GitHub.com. For more information, see "Configuring GitHub Copilot settings on GitHub.com". If you have allowed suggestions that match public code, GitHub Copilot can provide you with details about the matching code when you accept such suggestions. Matching code does not necessarily mean copyright infringement, so it is ultimately up to the user to determine whether to use the suggestion, and what and who to attribute (along with other license compliance) in appropriate circumstances.

#### Does GitHub Copilot include a filtering mechanism to mitigate risk?

Yes, GitHub Copilot does include an optional code referencing filter to detect and suppress certain suggestions that match public code on GitHub.

GitHub has created a duplication detection filter to detect and suppress suggestions that contain code segments over a certain length that match public code on GitHub. This filter can be enabled by the administrator for your enterprise and it can apply for all organizations within your enterprise, or the administrator can defer control to individual organizations.

With the filter enabled, Copilot checks code suggestions for matches or near-matches against public code on GitHub of 65 lexemes or more (on average,150 characters). If there is a match, the suggestion will not be shown to the user.

GitHub Copilot also includes filters to block offensive language in the prompts and to avoid synthesizing suggestions in sensitive contexts. We continue to work on improving the filter system to more intelligently detect and remove offensive outputs. If you see offensive outputs, please report them directly to copilot-safety@github.com so that we can improve our safeguards. GitHub takes this challenge very seriously and we are committed to addressing it.

In addition to off-topic, harmful, and offensive output filters, GitHub Copilot also scans the outputs for vulnerable code.

#### Can GitHub Copilot introduce insecure code in its suggestions?

Public code may contain insecure coding patterns, bugs, or references to outdated APIs or idioms. When GitHub Copilot synthesizes code suggestions based on this data, it can also synthesize code that contains these undesirable patterns. Copilot has filters in place that either block or notify users of insecure code patterns that are detected in Copilot suggestions. These filters target the most common vulnerable coding patterns, including hardcoded credentials, SQL injections, and path injections. Additionally, in recent years we’ve provided tools such as GitHub Advanced Security, GitHub Actions, Dependabot, and CodeQL to open source projects to help improve code quality. Of course, you should always use GitHub Copilot together with good testing and code review practices and security tools, as well as your own judgment.

#### Is GitHub Copilot intended to fully automate code generation and replace developers?

No. GitHub Copilot is a tool intended to make developers more efficient. It’s not intended to replace developers.

Developers should use exactly the same sorts of safeguards and diligence with Copilot’s suggestions as they would use with any third-party code.

Practices such as rigorous functionality testing, code scanning, security testing, etc. should continue policies with Copilot’s suggestions. Moreover, you should make sure your code editor or editor does not automatically compile or run generated code before you review it.

#### Does GitHub Copilot support accessibility features?

We are conducting internal testing of GitHub Copilot’s ease of use by developers with disabilities and working to ensure that GitHub Copilot is accessible to all developers. Learn more about accessibility at GitHub and view our detailed documentation on various accessibility topics and features, including instructions for using our products with screen readers and other assistive technologies at our GitHub Accessibility website.

#### Will GitHub Copilot work as well using languages other than English?

Given public sources are predominantly in English, GitHub Copilot will likely work less well in scenarios where natural language prompts provided by the developer are not in English and/or are grammatically incorrect. Therefore, non-English speakers might experience a lower quality of service.
